meta.name: Credit Counterfeit Index
meta.definition: CCI = Monetary Bind (mean z of HY OAS, SLOOS C&I tightening, real fed funds, inverted real M2 growth) minus Real Bind (genuine physical scarcity intensity). Credit is the counterfeiter when CCI >= threshold: tight money manufacturing scarcity that is not physically real.
meta.sources: Fed H.6 (M2, seasonally adjusted, August 2026: 5.7 percent year over year); FOMC target range 3.75-4.00 percent after the 16 September 2026 meeting; Fed Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, July 2026 (the October survey is not yet published); BEA core PCE, August 2026 (3.4 percent year over year; September not yet released); ICE BofA US High Yield OAS (3.40 on 25 October). Real Bind is a published judgment series (Strait of Hormuz transit conditions via IMF PortWatch, Brent, and the EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook of October 2026). FRED is not reachable from the build environment; series are sourced from the issuing agencies directly.
meta.projection_note: No quarter is currently projected. The September 2026 scenario for Q4 was wrong on the Real Bind, which is the dominant term in this index and the one least amenable to forecast. Near-term sensitivities are stated in the revision note instead.
meta.revision_note:
2026-10-25 update, and it closes the Q4 projection out as wrong on the term that matters. The September entry projected Q4 at -1.20 on a Real Bind of 1.20, assuming the Oman track would take heat out of the chokepoint without restoring open transit. The heat did not come out. The Strait is in its 237th day effectively closed, IMF PortWatch logged 4 transits on 18 October against a pre-crisis baseline near 85 a day, October set a record for ship attacks, and a tanker was struck on the 22nd. Brent settled near $116.72, about 17 percent above a month earlier and against the $104.6 that set the September reading.

The evidence is not all one way, which is why the Real Bind goes to 1.35 rather than higher. The EIA October Short-Term Energy Outlook puts regional shut-in production at 4.8 million barrels a day in September, down from 5.8 in August and 10.9 at the May peak, with exports recovering through bypass routes and ship-to-ship transfers. Transit counts and the spot price say escalation. The physical production measure says the disruption has more than halved since spring. This series names transit conditions and Brent ahead of the STEO, so the reading rises, but the shut-in trend caps how far it can honestly go. Weighting the physical measure more heavily gives 1.25 and a CCI of -1.26; weighting the chokepoint more gives 1.45 and -1.46. Brent at $117 is already $12 above the EIA's own fourth-quarter forecast of $105, which is itself a sign that the market is pricing a risk the supply balance does not capture.

The monetary side moved for the first time in three quarters, and only just. High yield OAS widened from 2.70 to 3.40, a 17-month high on 23 October, as an artificial intelligence equity selloff pushed investors toward haven assets and CCC spreads went out 43 basis points to 1,340. The 16 September hike to 3.75-4.00 percent, the first since 2023, lifted the real funds rate from 0.33 to 0.48 against core PCE of 3.4 percent. Real M2 growth is 2.3. Together that carries the Monetary Bind from -0.09 to -0.01, of which the spread widening contributed 0.07 and the hike 0.02. The SLOOS is unchanged at 3 because it is the same July survey; the October one is not yet published.

The index reads -1.36 for 2026Q4, against the -1.20 projected in September. Quarter over quarter it falls from -1.24, which reverses the Q3 improvement and returns the series exactly to its Q2 level. The mechanism is unchanged and bears repeating: every move in this series comes from the Real Bind, while the monetary side sits near zero and does almost nothing.

Nothing is projected forward this time. The September scenario failed on the Real Bind, and publishing another one as a dated data point would repeat the error rather than learn from it. The two near-term sensitivities can be stated without a projection. A 25 basis point hike at the 27-28 October meeting, which the September dot plot carries as the median, would take the real funds rate to 0.73 and the index to -1.32. The October SLOOS publishes in early November and is the first chance for the bank lending channel to confirm or contradict the spread widening.
meta.known_limitation: The Monetary Bind is built from aggregate inputs and cannot see the distribution beneath them. The July 2026 SLOOS is the clearest illustration: banks eased loan rate spreads for large and middle-market firms while a net share tightened credit card standards, and the aggregate C&I reading was 'basically unchanged'. A distributional companion is proposed but not yet scored, because no consistent history exists back to 2006. A second limitation is now visible in the series itself: the Real Bind is a quarterly judgment about physical constraint, and a chokepoint can reverse inside a quarter faster than the series can honestly be rescored. The August reading treated a partial reopening as a trend and was wrong. A third limitation is visible this quarter. The SLOOS is published about five weeks after a quarter opens, so when credit reprices mid-quarter for reasons outside bank lending standards, as it did in October 2026 on an equity selloff, the Monetary Bind registers the move only through the spread input and carries a stale survey for the rest of the quarter.
